findings.title: [P1] Inverted guard lets NaN and Infinity bypass timeout validation
findings.body: The new guard `Number.isFinite(timeout) && (...)` short-circuits to `false` when `Number(value)` yields a non-finite value, so the `throw` is skipped and the raw value is returned. Concretely: `parseTimeout("abc")` now returns `NaN` (old code: `parseInt("abc") === NaN` → threw `"invalid timeout"`), and `parseTimeout("Infinity")` / `parseTimeout("1e999")` return `Infinity` (old code threw). This breaks the function's core contract — successful results were previously guaranteed to be positive safe integers — for the most realistic bad input there is: any non-numeric string. Downstream, a `NaN`/`Infinity` timeout handed to `setTimeout` is coerced to a 1 ms delay (or disables the timeout in HTTP-client configs), turning invalid configuration into silent misbehavior. The fix is to negate the finite check: `if (!Number.isFinite(timeout) || !Number.isSafeInteger(timeout) || timeout <= 0) throw ...`.

findings.title: [P2] Number() swap changes accepted-input semantics from parseInt
findings.body: Replacing `Number.parseInt(value, 10)` with `Number(value)` changes observable results for inputs that previously parsed fine, contradicting the PR's stated intent to preserve existing contracts: `"12.5"` returned `12` but now throws; `"1e3"` returned `1` but now returns `1000`; `"1e-3"` returned `1` but now throws. Conversely, previously-rejected forms are now accepted: `"0x10"` threw but now returns `16` (`"0b10"` similarly returns `2`). Some tightening (rejecting trailing garbage like `"10ms"`) is arguably an improvement, but the divergent outcomes for decimal, exponent, and radix-prefixed strings should be an explicit, confirmed decision rather than a side effect — especially with no tests in the repo pinning this behavior.
